segments.t: At the start of this episode, Chef Barinov feeds his fish Arkady before welcoming Alexey Smolin, a Michelin inspector visiting the restaurant. Even after an awkward spill, the inspector praises the chef's signature tasting menu.
Now let's go back through their conversation line by line and unpack the Russian phrasing.
'Do not look at me like that.' Barinov picks one pointed expression for the inspector: "smotri" means "look" (from "smotret"), giving the line its exact edge.

'You must not be overfed right now.' Barinov sends the reaction for the inspector: the single Russian word "nelzya" ("it is not allowed, one must not") sets up the whole statement without needing a separate word for "it is".
'Hello, Viktor Petrovich.' The inspector continues warmly across the room, letting the remark speak for itself.
'I am inspecting your restaurant.' The inspector stresses one loaded piece with Barinov: "inspektiruyu" means "I inspect" (from "inspektirovat"), giving the line its exact edge.
'Is everything alright with you?' Barinov voices that point frankly here: notice how Russian needs no word for "am", "is", or "are" in the present — placing the words side by side says it all.
'Yes, it is just so unexpected.' The inspector reacts firmly facing Barinov, watching Barinov's face to see how the news lands.
'Hello, I am very pleased to meet you.' Barinov highlights one practical detail at once: "zdravstvuyte" means "hello", and it carries the main weight of what Barinov is saying.

'Your signature set is simply excellent.' The inspector brings the comment before Barinov: the little word "prosto" ("simply, just") works like a shrug in the sentence, making a big claim sound effortless.
'It overshadowed that unpleasant incident.' The inspector pushes back dryly to settle things, watching Barinov's face to see how the news lands.
'Thank you for the kind words.' Barinov grounds this sharp element with the inspector: "spasibo" means "thank you", and it carries the main weight of what Barinov is saying.
'Just do not worry.' Barinov gives this statement briskly now: the "-sya" ending on "volnuytes" ("worry") turns the action inward or makes it happen between people naturally.
'We will wash everything out quickly.' Barinov fires back openly to settle things, making his position completely clear.
The Michelin inspector seems genuinely impressed by the tasting menu, though trouble is just around the corner in the kitchen. Until next time!
